title: Intrinsic decay length in elastic localization
abstract: Localization in finite elastic structures is often studied using infinite-domain solutions, which avoid the explicit treatment of boundaries and admit simpler analytical descriptions. Yet it remains poorly understood when finite-domain localized states can be accurately approximated by their infinite-domain counterparts. In this work, we show that the accuracy is controlled by an intrinsic decay length. Using a prototypical localization model, we show that finite-domain localized solutions converge exponentially to the corresponding infinite-domain localized solution once the structural length exceeds the intrinsic decay length. The intrinsic decay length also explains the markedly different validity regimes of finite- and infinite-domain weakly nonlinear approximations. It further has important implications for numerical computation, since once the structural length exceeds the intrinsic decay length, localized solutions corresponding to different domain lengths differ only by exponentially small quantities, making them increasingly difficult to distinguish numerically. The theoretical predictions are validated using two representative localization problems: bulging in membrane tubes and localized helical buckling in twisted rods. The present work provides a unified geometric framework for understanding localization transition, asymptotic validity, and numerical computation in elastic localization.
summary: This work establishes a rigorous criterion, the intrinsic decay length, to quantify when localized solutions in finite elastic structures approach their infinite-domain limits. By analyzing prototypical models from mechanics, it provides a unified framework explaining the convergence rate and the differing validity regimes of weakly nonlinear approximations in both finite and infinite settings.
main_problem: The core problem is determining when localized solutions in finite elastic structures can be accurately approximated by their simpler infinite-domain counterparts.
main_result: Convergence occurs exponentially once the structural length exceeds a characteristic intrinsic decay length, which governs the validity of both approximations and weakly nonlinear theories.
method: Theoretical analysis using phase-plane methods, asymptotic matching (inner/outer regions), and quantitative error estimation via Grönwall-type inequalities.
model_or_system: The study uses prototypical localization models derived from continuum mechanics, applied to physical systems like bulging in membrane tubes or helical buckling in twisted rods. The analysis compares solutions governed by periodic orbits (finite domain) to those governed by homoclinic orbits (infinite domain).
key_observables: Intrinsic decay length ($\ell_{dec}$), amplitude measures of localized deformation, and the difference between finite-domain and infinite-domain solution profiles.
important_parameters: Structural length ($L$), loading parameter ($\gamma$), and the intrinsic decay length ($\ell_{dec}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the system can be modeled by a prototypical nonlinear ODE, allowing for comparison between periodic (finite) and homoclinic (infinite) solutions.
figures_summary: Figures compare amplitude measures and centerline positions of localized states across varying loading parameters ($\gamma$), showing rapid convergence towards the infinite-domain solution as $\gamma$ decreases or $L$ increases relative to $\ell_{dec}$.
paper_structure: The paper develops a unified geometric framework by comparing finite-domain boundary value problems (periodic orbits) with their infinite-domain limits (homoclinic orbits). It applies this framework sequentially to membrane bulging and helical buckling, culminating in the definition of the intrinsic decay length.
why_interesting: While focused on classical elasticity, the mathematical machinery—comparing solutions based on different topological structures (periodic vs. homoclinic) and identifying a characteristic length scale ($\ell_{dec}$) that dictates the breakdown of approximations—is highly relevant to understanding crossover regimes in quantum systems or disordered media.
